paras: The attempted lynching of Joseph Erwin took place in East St. Louis, Illinois, on the afternoon of December 7, 1903, when a crowd of several hundred chased Erwin, a Black man accused of robbing and shooting a white man, and tried to seize him from a policeman. Policeman P. J. Mulqueeny held the crowd back with drawn revolvers until a patrol wagon took Erwin to the police station unharmed. Newspapers across the country carried the episode as a rescue of a man from a mob, and Erwin was later held for murder after the wounded man died.

According to the St. Louis Republic, Edward Lawson, a one-armed white man of 30, had come from Mount Vernon that morning with a youth, William Hall, to look for railroad work. Near the old East St. Louis race track they came upon Erwin and several boys cleaning fish caught in the slough. The Republic charged that Erwin drew a revolver, took $27 and Lawson's overcoat, and then shot him through the breast, and that he also wounded D. R. Bradley, a Black boy, in the back. The wire version instead said Erwin had tried to hold up men in a saloon and shot Lawson when he alone resisted.

Railroad men who heard of the shooting followed Erwin toward the center of the city, and the crowd grew with every block. At Tenth street and Tudor avenue Erwin ran into Mulqueeny, who grabbed him and knocked him down, while the crowd surrounded them shouting "Lynch the negro." Mulqueeny drew two revolvers, warned that he would shoot the first man who approached, and marched Erwin to Jackson's saloon, where a citizen telephoned for the patrol wagon.

For about half an hour the policeman stood in the saloon doorway with his revolvers leveled while the crowd swelled with hundreds more men and boys. Ropes were brought, and the Republic reported that some of the crowd had gone through rear yards and were ready to break into the back of the saloon when the wagon arrived. The wire put the crowd at two hundred and said the police "fought the mob off" and lodged him in jail on a minor charge pending the outcome of Lawson's wound.

At the station Erwin was identified by Hall, Bradley and others, though he denied his identity. Lawson died at St. Mary's Hospital in East St. Louis on the morning of December 9, and at the inquest that afternoon Erwin, identified as "alias Evans, a St. Louis negro," was held for murder after half a dozen men testified and he declined to take the stand. No report of an indictment or trial, or of any arrest among the crowd, appears in the coverage.

Coverage was found only in white papers, and the St. Louis Republic gave the fullest account, headlined "East St. Louis Mob Gives Long Chase in Attempt to Lynch Joseph Erwin" and "Policeman Holds Them Back." It stated the robbery and shooting as fact and made the policeman's stand the center of the story. Its follow-up two days later, "Negro Held for Lawson Murder," recalled that Mulqueeney "had a hard time keeping the crowd from lynching him."

A St. Louis wire story ran on December 8 in papers from Montgomery and Indianapolis to Fargo, Bennington and Waterbury, under headlines such as "Tried to Lynch Negro," "Negro Saved From a Mob by the Police" and "Almost Lynched." Shorter versions followed in Denison, Iowa, and Milbank, South Dakota, and a Texas paper reduced it to a single line: "St. Louis police kept Joe Irwin, a negro, from being lynched." The wire copy called him Joe Irvin or Joe Irwin, and the Indianapolis Journal's subhead described "a Negro Who Shot a White Man for Resisting Robbery."

The accounts differ on the man's name, his age, the setting of the robbery and whether Lawson came from Mount Vernon, Indiana, as the Republic said, or Mount Vernon, Illinois, as the wire said. The Republic, a local paper that also reported the inquest, set the robbery in the open near the race track, while the wire set the hold-up in a saloon.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Joseph Erwin
bases: A crowd of hundreds chased a Black man accused of shooting a white man, shouted 'Lynch the negro,' brought ropes and tried to reach him in a saloon where a policeman held him, but he was taken away unharmed (A1, A2, A4).

A mob of 200 to several hundred acted without authority to punish a man accused of robbery and shooting, but every account says he reached the police station unharmed (A1, A2, A4); it was an attempted lynching, not a killing.
The St. Louis Republic's local account (A1, A9) and the separately worded Associated wire (A2, A4) agree on the shooting, the mob, and the police rescue, though they differ on details.

framing.detail: The St. Louis Republic headlined 'East St. Louis Mob Gives Long Chase in Attempt to Lynch Joseph Erwin' and 'Policeman Holds Them Back,' stated the robbery and shooting as fact, and centered the policeman's stand.
Wire copy ran as rescue stories ('Tried to Lynch Negro', 'Negro Saved From Mob', 'Narrowly Escapes Lynching'), noting the man was landed 'unharmed' and that Lawson was not expected to live.
